title: Determinants
summary: How to compute determinants efficiently (cofactor expansion and row reduction), the algebraic rules det(AB) = det A det B and det(cA) = cⁿ det A, and the geometric meaning of |det| as the area/volume scaling factor of a linear map.

lesson.title: What a determinant is: cofactor expansion

blocks.text: For a 2×2 matrix, det [a b; c d] = ad − bc. For larger matrices we define det recursively.
Aᵢⱼ is A with row i and column j deleted. The (i, j)-cofactor is Cᵢⱼ = (−1)<sup>i+j</sup> det Aᵢⱼ.

blocks.name: Cofactor expansion
blocks.text: det A can be computed along ANY row i: det A = aᵢ₁Cᵢ₁ + aᵢ₂Cᵢ₂ + ⋯ + aᵢₙCᵢₙ, or down any column j: det A = a₁ⱼC₁ⱼ + ⋯ + aₙⱼCₙⱼ. All give the same number.
The sign pattern (−1)<sup>i+j</sup> is a checkerboard starting with + in the top-left:

blocks.name: Triangular matrices
blocks.text: If A is triangular (upper or lower), det A is the product of the diagonal entries.

proof.text: Expand down the first column (or along the first row) repeatedly: only the diagonal entry survives each time.

blocks.text: Always expand along the row or column with the most zeros: each zero kills a whole sub-determinant.

blocks.title: Cofactor expansion along the best row/column
steps: Row 3 has a single nonzero entry, 5, in position (3, 3), sign (−1)⁶ = +.
In that 3×3, column 2 has a single nonzero entry −1 at (2, 2), sign +: det = −1·det [2 3; 3 1] = −1·(2 − 9) = 7.

blocks.text: Concretely for 3×3, expanding along row 1: det A = a₁₁(a₂₂a₃₃ − a₂₃a₃₂) − a₁₂(a₂₁a₃₃ − a₂₃a₃₁) + a₁₃(a₂₁a₃₂ − a₂₂a₃₁). For larger n cofactor expansion costs about n! multiplications, which is why we expand only along sparse rows and otherwise row reduce (about n³ operations).

blocks.title: A 5×5 determinant in two steps (exam-hard)
steps: Row 3 has one nonzero entry, 5 at (3, 3), sign (−1)⁶ = +: det A = 5·det B, B = A without row 3 and column 3 = [3 0 0 1; 1 2 −1 0; 2 0 3 0; 0 0 0 2].
In B, row 4 has one nonzero entry, 2 at (4, 4), sign +: det B = 2·det [3 0 0; 1 2 −1; 2 0 3].
Expand that along row 1: 3·(2·3 − (−1)·0) = 18. So det B = 36.

blocks.name: Effect of row operations
blocks.text: (a) Replacement (add a multiple of one row to another): det unchanged. (b) Interchange of two rows: det changes sign. (c) Scaling a row by k: det is multiplied by k.

proof.text: Intuition from volume: det measures the signed volume of the box spanned by the rows. A shear (replacement) slides one edge parallel to the others, keeping base and height, so the volume is unchanged. Scaling one edge by k scales volume by k. A swap reverses orientation, which flips the sign.

Algebraically: (b) is proved by induction, expanding along a row not involved in the swap; (a) follows from (b), (c) and linearity in a row: det with row rⱼ + c·rᵢ = det(original) + c·det(matrix with two equal rows rᵢ), and a matrix with two equal rows has det 0 because swapping them changes the sign but not the matrix.

blocks.title: Determinant by row reduction
items: Reduce A to an echelon form U using replacements and interchanges (avoid scaling, or record it).
Count the interchanges r.
det A = (−1)ʳ·(product of the diagonal of U), times any factors you pulled out by scaling.

blocks.title: Row reduction with a swap
steps: Triangular: product of diagonal = 1·3·(−5) = −15. One swap ⇒ det A = −(−15).

blocks.title: Row reduction with a factored-out scalar

blocks.text: Do not confuse 'scale a row by k' (det × k) with 'det(kA)' (every row scaled: det × kⁿ).

blocks.name: Column operations
blocks.text: det Aᵀ = det A, so column operations affect det exactly as the corresponding row operations do. A matrix with a zero row or column, or two equal (or proportional) rows or columns, has det 0.

blocks.name: Linearity in one row
blocks.text: If all rows but row i are fixed, det is a linear function of row i: det[…, u + v, …] = det[…, u, …] + det[…, v, …] and det[…, cu, …] = c·det[…, u, …]. (It is NOT linear in the whole matrix: det(A + B) ≠ det A + det B.)

proof.text: Expand along row i: det A = Σⱼ aᵢⱼCᵢⱼ, and the cofactors Cᵢⱼ do not involve row i at all.

blocks.title: Track several operations at once (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: If det [a b c; d e f; g h i] = 7, find det [d e f; 3a 3b 3c; g − 2a h − 2b i − 2c].
steps: Start from the original (det 7). Swap rows 1 and 2: det becomes −7.
Scale the new row 2 (= old row 1) by 3: det becomes −21.
Replace row 3 by row 3 − 2·(old row 1): replacement, det unchanged. (Subtracting a multiple of the old row 1 is legal even though that row is now scaled: it is a multiple of the current row 2.)

blocks.name: Invertibility
blocks.text: A square matrix A is invertible ⇔ det A ≠ 0.

proof.text: Row reduce to echelon form U with det A = ±(nonzero factors)·det U. A is invertible ⇔ U has n pivots ⇔ every diagonal entry of U is nonzero ⇔ det U ≠ 0.

blocks.name: Multiplicative property
blocks.text: det(AB) = (det A)(det B).

proof.text: If A is singular, so is AB, and both sides are 0. Otherwise A is a product of elementary matrices, and det(EB) = det(E)·det(B) for each elementary E by the row-operation rules.

items: det Aᵀ = det A.
det A⁻¹ = 1/det A (from det A · det A⁻¹ = det I = 1).
det(cA) = cⁿ det A for n×n A (each of the n rows is scaled by c).
det(Aᵏ) = (det A)ᵏ; det(AB) = det(BA) even though AB ≠ BA.
det(A + B) ≠ det A + det B in general.

blocks.title: Using the properties
blocks.prompt: A and B are 3×3 with det A = 4 and det B = −2. Find det(2A), det(A⁻¹B²), det(AᵀB), det(−A), det(B⁻¹AB).

blocks.text: det(cA) uses cⁿ, not c. For a 4×4 matrix, det(−A) = +det A.

blocks.title: Unknown determinant from a matrix equation (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: A is a 3×3 invertible matrix with A³ = 4A. Find all possible values of det A. Then find det(2A⁻¹Aᵀ) for each.
steps: Take determinants: (det A)³ = det(4A) = 4³ det A = 64 det A.
det A ≠ 0 (invertible), so (det A)² = 64 ⇒ det A = ±8.
det(2A⁻¹Aᵀ) = 2³·(1/det A)·det A = 8 for either value.

blocks.text: det(4A) = 4ⁿ det A with n = 3 here, not 4 det A.
Similar matrices B = P⁻¹AP have det B = det A, so the determinant is a property of the linear transformation, not of the basis chosen.

lesson.title: Parameters that make a determinant zero

blocks.text: 'For which values of h is A singular (non-invertible / columns dependent / Ax = 0 nontrivial)?' all mean: solve det A = 0.

blocks.title: Parameter making det 0
blocks.prompt: For which h is A = [1 2 3; 2 h 4; 3 5 7] not invertible?
steps: Cofactor expansion along row 1: det A = 1(7h − 20) − 2(14 − 12) + 3(10 − 3h).
blocks.answer: A is singular exactly when h = 3.

blocks.text: Factor rather than expand when you can: use row operations to pull out common factors (e.g. add all rows together if row sums are equal). A 3×3 det that is a cubic in h may have up to 3 roots; make sure you find all.

blocks.title: Equal row sums trick
blocks.prompt: For which x is the 4×4 matrix with x on the diagonal and 1 elsewhere singular?
steps: Add rows 2, 3, 4 to row 1: row 1 becomes (x + 3)(1, 1, 1, 1). Factor out x + 3.
Subtract the all-ones row from rows 2–4: they become (x − 1) times standard rows; the matrix is triangular with diagonal 1, x − 1, x − 1, x − 1.

blocks.title: Characteristic-equation preview (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: For which λ is A − λI singular, where A = [2 1 0; 1 2 0; 0 0 3]?
steps: det(A − λI) = det [2−λ 1 0; 1 2−λ 0; 0 0 3−λ]. Expand along row 3 (two zeros): (3 − λ)[(2 − λ)² − 1].
blocks.answer: λ = 1 or λ = 3 (these are the eigenvalues of A)

blocks.name: Geometric meaning
blocks.text: If A is 2×2, |det A| is the area of the parallelogram spanned by its columns. If A is 3×3, |det A| is the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by its columns.

proof.text: Column operations of replacement type (shears) do not change area (same base, same height) and do not change det; reduce to a diagonal matrix, where the box is a rectangle with area |product of diagonal|.

blocks.name: Scaling under T
blocks.text: If T(x) = Ax and S is a region of finite area (volume), then area(T(S)) = |det A|·area(S).
This is why det(AB) = det A · det B: applying B scales areas by |det B|, then A scales them by |det A|; the sign tracks whether orientation is reversed.

blocks.title: Area of a parallelogram and of its image
blocks.prompt: Find the area of the parallelogram with vertices (−1, 0), (1, 5), (3, 1), (5, 6). Then find the area of its image under T(x) = [1 2; 0 3]x.
steps: det [1 2; 0 3] = 3, so the image has area 3·18.

blocks.title: Volume and image of the unit ball
blocks.prompt: Find the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by (1, 2, 0), (0, 1, 3), (2, 0, 1), and the area of the image of the unit disk under T(x) = [2 1; −1 3]x.

blocks.text: Use edge vectors (differences of vertices), not the vertices themselves. Triangles have half the parallelogram area. Volumes use |det|.

blocks.title: Triangle, tetrahedron, ellipse (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: (a) Area of the triangle with vertices (1, 2), (3, 1), (4, 5). (b) Volume of the tetrahedron with vertices 0, (1, 2, 1), (2, 0, 1), (3, 1, 4). (c) Area of the image of the unit disk under T(x) = [2 1; 1 3]x.
steps: (a) Edges from (1, 2): (2, −1) and (3, 3). |det [2 3; −1 3]| = |6 + 3| = 9. A triangle is half a parallelogram: 9/2.
(b) A tetrahedron is 1/6 of the parallelepiped on the same edges: |det [1 2 3; 2 0 1; 1 1 4]| = |−9| = 9, volume 9/6 = 3/2.
(c) det = 6 − 1 = 5, so area = 5·π·1² = 5π (the image is an ellipse).

blocks.text: The sign of det tells orientation: det > 0 keeps the counterclockwise order of e₁, e₂; det < 0 flips it (a mirror image). det = 0 means the image is flattened into a line or a point, which is exactly why A is not invertible: information is lost.

blocks.title: Combine scaling factors (routine)
blocks.prompt: T rotates the plane by 30° and then stretches horizontally by 3. A region S has area 4. Find the area of T(S) and decide whether T preserves orientation.

blocks.text: Why |det| scales every region: approximate the region by tiny squares. T maps each square to a parallelogram whose area is |det A| times the square's area (the columns of A, scaled), and summing gives area(T(S)) = |det A|·area(S).

blocks.title: Decision procedure for det A
items: 2×2: ad − bc. 3×3 with no zeros: row 1 expansion (or Sarrus) is fine.
A row or column with one nonzero entry: expand along it immediately.
Triangular (or block triangular): multiply the diagonal (or the block determinants).
Otherwise: use replacements to create zeros in one column, then expand along that column. Replacements cost nothing; swaps flip the sign; record any scaling.
Spot dependence first: two proportional rows/columns, or a row that is a combination of others, gives 0 instantly.

blocks.title: Mix row reduction with expansion
steps: Clear column 1 below the pivot with replacements (det unchanged): R₂ − 2R₁ → [0 1 2 3], R₃ + R₁ → [0 2 2 3], R₄ − 3R₁ → [0 0 0 1].
Expand that along its last row (one nonzero entry, sign +): 1·det [1 2; 2 2] = 2 − 4 = −2.

blocks.name: Proof idea of det(AB) = det A · det B
blocks.text: For an elementary matrix E, det(EB) = det E · det B: this is exactly the row-operation rule (det E is 1, −1 or c for replacement, swap, scaling). If A is invertible, A = E₁E₂⋯Eₖ, so det(AB) = det E₁ ⋯ det Eₖ · det B = det A · det B. If A is singular, AB is singular too (rank AB ≤ rank A < n), so both sides are 0.

Background (useful for theory): the cofactor formula for the inverse, A⁻¹ = (1/det A)·adj A, where adj A is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors. It explains why a matrix of integers with det = ±1 has an integer inverse, and why entries of A⁻¹ are 'cofactor over determinant'.

blocks.title: One entry of A⁻¹ from a cofactor
blocks.prompt: For A = [1 2 0; 0 1 3; 2 0 1], find det A and the (1, 3) entry of A⁻¹.
steps: (A⁻¹)₁₃ = C₃₁/det A (note the transposed indices). C₃₁ = (−1)⁴ det [2 0; 1 3] = 6.

hard.title: Determinant of xI + (ones) and its rank

prompt.text: Compute det A for the 4×4 matrix with x on the diagonal and 1 everywhere else. For which x is A singular, and what is rank A in each case?

hard.answer: det A = (x + 3)(x − 1)³; singular at x = 1 (rank 1) and x = −3 (rank 3); otherwise rank 4

solution.title: Solution
items: Add rows 2, 3, 4 to row 1: row 1 becomes (x+3)(1, 1, 1, 1). Factor out x + 3 (scaling rule).
Subtract the new row 1 (all ones) from rows 2–4: they become (0, x−1, 0, 0), (0, 0, x−1, 0), (0, 0, 0, x−1). Triangular.
x = 1: all entries 1, rank 1. x = −3: rank 3 (nullity 1, Nul = Span{(1,1,1,1)}). Otherwise rank 4.

solution.text: What it tests: Row sums are all equal ⇒ add all rows into one. The multiplicity of a root of det does not directly give the nullity, but here it happens to (symmetric matrix).

solution.title: Solution

hard.title: Vandermonde determinant
hard.answer: Row ops + expansion give (b − a)(c − a)(c − b)

solution.title: Solution
items: R₂ − R₁, R₃ − R₁: rows (0, b−a, b²−a²), (0, c−a, c²−a²). det unchanged.
Expand along column 1: det = (b−a)(c²−a²) − (c−a)(b²−a²).

solution.text: What it tests: Factor before expanding. Consequence: through 3 points with distinct t-values there is exactly one quadratic.

prompt.text: Construct a 3×3 matrix with integer entries, no zero entries, and determinant 1. Then explain (without computing) why its inverse has integer entries, and find the inverse.

solution.text: . Row reduce: R₂ − R₁, R₃ − R₁ → (0,1,1), (0,1,2); R₃ − R₂ → (0,0,1). Triangular with diagonal 1,1,1 and only replacements used ⇒ det = 1.
A⁻¹ = adj(A)/1 and cofactors of an integer matrix are integers.

What it tests: Building from a triangular matrix with unit diagonal by replacements guarantees det 1 — a reliable way to manufacture examples.

hard.title: Skew-symmetric matrices of odd size

prompt.text: A is 5×5 with Aᵀ = −A. Prove det A = 0. Is the same true for 4×4 skew-symmetric matrices?

hard.answer: det A = (−1)⁵ det A ⇒ det A = 0; false for 4×4 (e.g. block-diagonal [0 1; −1 0] has det 1)

solution.text: det A = det Aᵀ = det(−A) = (−1)⁵ det A = −det A.
So 2 det A = 0 ⇒ det A = 0. ∎
For even n the argument gives det A = det A, no information — and it’s false:
has det 1, and the 4×4 block-diagonal version of it also has det 1.
What it tests: The key is (−1)ⁿ with n odd. Students who write det(−A) = −det A without the dimension lose the 4×4 part.

hard.title: Tridiagonal determinant recursion

prompt.text: Let Dₙ be the determinant of the n×n tridiagonal matrix with 2 on the diagonal and −1 directly above and below it. Show Dₙ = 2Dₙ₋₁ − Dₙ₋₂ and conclude Dₙ = n + 1.

hard.answer: Dₙ = 2Dₙ₋₁ − Dₙ₋₂ with D₁ = 2, D₂ = 3 ⇒ Dₙ = n + 1

solution.title: Solution
items: Expand along row 1 (only two nonzero entries): Dₙ = 2·C₁₁ + (−1)·C₁₂, where C₁₁ = Dₙ₋₁ and C₁₂ = (−1)¹⁺²M₁₂.
Deleting row 1 and column 2 leaves a matrix whose first column is (−1, 0, …, 0)ᵀ; expanding down it gives M₁₂ = (−1)·Dₙ₋₂. So C₁₂ = Dₙ₋₂ and the second term is −Dₙ₋₂.
So Dₙ = 2Dₙ₋₁ − Dₙ₋₂, with D₁ = 2, D₂ = 3.
Induction: if Dₙ₋₁ = n and Dₙ₋₂ = n − 1 then Dₙ = 2n − (n − 1) = n + 1. ∎ (Checked for n ≤ 7.)

solution.text: What it tests: Track cofactor signs carefully: it’s (−1)<sup>i+j</sup> times the entry times the minor. The second expansion is down a column with one nonzero entry.

parsons.title: Invertible ⇔ nonzero determinant (one direction)
parsons.goal: Prove: if A is invertible, then det A ≠ 0 and det(A⁻¹) = 1/det A.
lines: Since A is invertible, AA⁻¹ = I.
By the multiplicative property, det(AA⁻¹) = det A · det(A⁻¹).
A product equal to 1 has no zero factor, so det A ≠ 0.
distractors: By the additive property, det(AA⁻¹) = det A + det A⁻¹.

parsons.title: Odd skew-symmetric matrices are singular
parsons.goal: Prove: if A is 5×5 and Aᵀ = −A, then det A = 0.
lines: det A = det Aᵀ, since transposing does not change the determinant.
det(−A) = (−1)⁵ det A, since all 5 rows are multiplied by −1.
Hence 2 det A = 0, i.e. det A = 0. ∎
distractors: det(−A) = −det A for every square matrix.

parsons.title: Similar matrices have equal determinants
parsons.goal: Prove: if B = P⁻¹AP with P invertible, then det B = det A.
lines: By multiplicativity, det(P⁻¹AP) = det(P⁻¹)·det A·det P.
So det B = (1/det P)·det A·det P.
The factors det P cancel (det P ≠ 0), so det B = det A. ∎
distractors: So det B = det A only when P = I.
